Case A

A1: The search of the past seven days returned only the earlier requests from the stable region. That shows no earlier misuse in those seven days. The key was published at some point, though, and the window may not cover the whole period since publication, and the search covers only that key's logged requests. The burst came 19 minutes after publication, and the seven-day window includes the time since publication. If the window covers publication through the burst, nothing came before the burst except the legitimate-looking requests. So the burst was the first misuse seen, and the answer is "Yes", though this rests on the search being complete. The statement says the search returned only those earlier requests, so the burst appears to be the first. The remaining risk is that misuse was not logged. I answer "Yes".

A2: The check scored the account at 30 minutes, after the burst at 19 minutes. We don't know what evidence the check had access to or what features it uses. So "Cannot tell".

A3: A shared destination is attached to three accounts. That is not enough to establish a single owner, since it could be a shared bank, a processor, or an attacker's destination. "No, not by itself".

A4: No reports after 30 days is weak evidence at best, and it is not clear anyone would have reported. "Cannot tell" fits, but "Yes, weakly" is also arguable. The absence of any finding doesn't say whether anyone looked, so I choose "Cannot tell".

A5: The burst involved a new fingerprint, a residential proxy, and changes to the payout destination and schedule. This warrants investigation: "Yes".

Case B

B1: D has 0 chargebacks against 2 for the others, on 100 transactions each, so D's recorded rate is 0% versus 2%. The recorded rate is lower, so "Yes". Small numbers make the difference weak, but the question asks about the rate.

B2: The combined measure is 5 percent, and it includes alerts. A combined figure doesn't show that no single account is above 5 percent. Chargebacks alone are 6 of 400, or 1.5%, so the 5 percent must include alerts, which could be concentrated in one account. "No".

B3: The search found no accounts beyond A and the closed account. That only covers the identifiers searched, so it doesn't show the person has no other accounts. "No".

B4: The two notes say the same thing, but their independence is unclear. They were written by different analysts on different days, but we can't tell whether they used the same evidence or one read the other. "Cannot tell".

B5: A blocked payment with no chargeback isn't a confirmed non-fraud transaction, because the block prevented the chargeback. "No".

B6: Shared templates and descriptor patterns, along with the person's links, justify a joint investigation: "Yes".

RESULT CN-015 | A1: Yes | A2: Cannot tell | A3: No, not by itself | A4: Cannot tell | A5: Yes | B1: Yes | B2: No | B3: No | B4: Cannot tell | B5: No | B6: Yes
